title: The launch master's notebook from Gray Reach
public_context: A launch master keeps a personal notebook about a fictional rowing club's annual regatta. The document is an event-day account in a familiar water-sport setting, written from the perspective of someone working on the course. The crews and setting are invented.
source_title: Notebook entry from the Gray Reach regatta
source_text:
I was in the launch for the fourth Gray Reach regatta, carrying the spare flag and the judge's clipboard. The course ran from the old ferry steps to a white post above the bend, then back to the landing. Senior pairs and junior fours started in separate divisions, each crew released thirty seconds after the one ahead. The senior pairs finished before the white float slipped below the post, although the current had been drawing its short chain toward the bank by the final turn.

The judge raised the black flag from our launch and held the junior fours at the steps. No boat was told to restart from the water. We pulled the float ashore and found that its chain link had opened; the post itself had not moved. The club steward brought a heavier chain from the boat shed, and the judge waited until the float held steady before releasing the junior crews.

The junior fours rowed the same course from the steps to the post and back. Their clocks started when each bow crossed the chalk line, not when the launch sounded its horn. The senior pairs already on the result board kept their first-division places, but the judge did not compare their elapsed times with the junior times. The steward explained that pairs and fours were separate boat classes, with different crew counts, so the clocks belonged on separate result pages.

A senior pair from East Quay finished first in its division, and the two junior crews from Ash Bend took first and second in theirs. No hull touched another boat or the bank. The judge awarded division ribbons but did not name a single fastest club across both divisions. The result sheet lists each division on its own page, with a pencil note beside the senior times: “marker drift; no cross-division comparison.”

When we carried the spare chain back to the shed, the steward asked me to keep the opened link with the clipboard until the committee meeting. The crews had already loaded their boats onto trailers, and the next regatta on the calendar was the autumn river clean-up row.
